import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Packing

This file contains a number of open problems related to the minimal size of a square (or circle)
that can contain a given number of unit squares (or circles).
In each case, we provide a known upper bound, and ask for the least such size.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia on packing of squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing)
- [Wikipedia on packing of circles in a circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_packing_in_a_circle)
- [Wikipedia on packing of circles in a square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_packing_in_a_square)
- Friedman, Erich (2009), "Packing unit squares in squares: a survey and new results",
  Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 1000, Dynamic Survey 7
- Pirl, U. (1969),
  ["Der Mindestabstand von $n$ in der Einheitskreisscheibe gelegenen Punkten"](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.19690400110),
  Mathematische Nachrichten, 40: 111–124
- A website with visualizations of packings:
  [link](https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/)
-/

open EuclideanGeometry

open scoped NNReal

universe u

namespace SquarePacking

/--
A square of a particular side length as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
Not including border, so that squares that touch at the border are disjoint,
but a square internal to another shape is a subset of that shape.
-/
def Square (side : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  {p : ℝ² | 0 < p 0 ∧ p 0 < side ∧ 0 < p 1 ∧ p 1 < side}

/--
The unit square as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
-/
def UnitSquare : Set ℝ² := Square 1

/--
A circle of a particular radius as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
The radius is a nonnegative real, so that `Circle r` is always the disc of radius $r$.
Not including border, so that circles that touch at the border are disjoint,
but a circle internal to another shape is a subset of that shape.
-/
def Circle (r : ℝ≥0) : Set ℝ² :=
  {p : ℝ² | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 < (r : ℝ) ^ 2}

/--
The unit circle as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
-/
def UnitCircle : Set ℝ² := Circle 1

/--
A structure representing a packing of `n` isometric embeddings
of a set `s` inside a (presumably larger) set `S`.
-/
structure Packing (n : ℕ) (s : Set ℝ²) (S : Set ℝ²) where
  /-- The isometric equivalences
  that represent the transformations of the base shape to their locations in the packing. -/
  embeddings : Fin n → (ℝ² ≃ᵢ ℝ²)
  /-- The images of the embeddings are pairwise disjoint -/
  disjoint : Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (embeddings i '' s) (embeddings j '' s)
  /-- The images of the embeddings are all inside the larger set `S` -/
  inside : ∀ i : Fin n, embeddings i '' s ⊆ S

/--
The degenerate circle is empty.
-/
@[category test, AMS 51]
theorem circle_zero : Circle 0 = ∅ := by
  ext p
  simp only [Circle, Set.mem_ofPred_eq, Set.mem_empty_iff_false, iff_false, not_lt,
    NNReal.coe_zero, zero_pow, ne_eq, OfNat.ofNat_ne_zero, not_false_eq_true]
  positivity

/--
Eleven unit squares can be packed into a square of side length < 3.877084.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem eleven_square_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square 3.877084)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 11 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_eleven_square_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Seventeen unit squares can be packed into a square of side length < 4.6756.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem seventeen_square_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square 4.6756)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 17 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_seventeen_square_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Three unit squares can be packed into a circle of radius $(5 \sqrt{17}) / 16 \approx 1.288$.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_circle)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem three_square_packing_in_circle_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 3 UnitSquare (Circle ((5 * NNReal.sqrt 17) / 16))) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest circle that can contain 3 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_circle)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_three_square_packing_in_circle :
    IsLeast {r : ℝ≥0 | Nonempty (Packing 3 UnitSquare (Circle r))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Twenty-one unit circles can be packed into a square of side length < 9.359.

Reference: [Visualizations](https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem twenty_one_circle_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square 9.359)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 21 unit circles?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_twenty_one_circle_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Fifteen unit circles can be packed into a circle of radius
$1 + \sqrt{6 + 2/\sqrt{5} + 4 \sqrt{1 + 2/\sqrt{5}}} \approx 4.521$.

Reference:
Graham RL, Lubachevsky BD, Nurmela KJ, Ostergard PRJ.
Dense packings of congruent circles in a circle. Discrete Math 1998;181:139–154.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem fifteen_circle_packing_in_circle_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 15 UnitCircle
      (Circle (1 + NNReal.sqrt (6 + 2 / NNReal.sqrt 5 +
        4 * NNReal.sqrt (1 + 2 / NNReal.sqrt 5))))) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest circle that can contain 15 unit circles?

Reference:
Graham RL, Lubachevsky BD, Nurmela KJ, Ostergard PRJ.
Dense packings of congruent circles in a circle. Discrete Math 1998;181:139–154.
[Pirl (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.19690400110) conjectured this configuration to be optimal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_fifteen_circle_packing_in_circle :
    IsLeast {r : ℝ≥0 | Nonempty (Packing 15 UnitCircle (Circle r))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end SquarePacking

findings.description: The docstring promises a square with side length strictly less than 3.877084, whereas the Lean type asserts a packing in `Square 3.877084`, giving a non-strict upper bound. Using an open square does not impose strict slack: boundary-touching packings are permitted. The numerical upper bound itself is correct.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia, Square_packing#In_a_square, describes Trump's packing with side approximately 3.877084. The current table linked from Friedman's packing site gives approximately 3.87708359002281 for n = 11 (https://kingbird.myphotos.cc/packing/squares_in_squares.html), which also supports the stronger strict bound stated in the docstring.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to say 'of side length 3.877084' or 'of side length at most 3.877084'. Alternatively, retain the strict wording and state `∃ x : ℝ, x < 3.877084 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square x))`.

findings.description: The docstring states a strict upper bound, side length < 4.6756, but `Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square 4.6756))` only asserts packing at the displayed side length. Open interiors allow contact with the container boundary and do not make this a strict size bound. The asserted non-strict bound is valid.
findings.source_evidence: Friedman's cited survey, Section 3, Figure 12, explicitly states `s(17) < 4.6756` (https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/DS7/html_1). Ellsworth's linked table gives Bidwell's packing side as approximately 4.67553009360455.
findings.suggested_fix: Use 'of side length 4.6756' or 'at most 4.6756' in the docstring, or strengthen the statement to `∃ x : ℝ, x < 4.6756 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square x))`.

findings.description: The docstring promises a containing square of side length strictly less than 9.359, but the theorem asserts a packing in `Square 9.359`. This supplies a non-strict upper bound, not the strict inequality in the prose. The displayed bound is safely above the known packing size.
findings.source_evidence: The cited visualization page gives `s = 9.358+` for 21 unit circles (https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/). Its linked Packomania table gives the more precise side length 9.3580199589 (https://www.packomania.com/csq/csq.html).
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to 'of side length 9.359' or 'at most 9.359', or state `∃ x : ℝ, x < 9.359 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square x))`.

status_issues.source_status: Solved by Nurmela and Östergård in 1999. The minimum side length for 21 unit-radius circles is approximately 9.3580199589.
status_issues.evidence: The directly cited Friedman visualization labels n = 21 'Proved by Nurmela and Östergård in 1999' (https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/). Their paper, More Optimal Packings of Equal Circles in a Square, extends proved optimality through n = 27 and discusses the special n = 21 proof on p. 450. Table 2 gives d₂₁ ≈ 0.2718122553; the unit-circle side length is 2 + 2/d₂₁. PDF: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/PL00009472.pdf.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to `research solved` and cite the 1999 optimality proof. An answer can be supplied using an exact characterization of the known optimum; neither 9.359 nor its decimal approximation should be used as an exact answer.

reformulations.difference: The file packs open squares and disks into open containers, rather than closed geometric pieces with disjoint interiors and boundary contact allowed.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let A be a closed unit square or unit disk and C a closed square or disk container. The file's shapes are their interiors, and A = closure (interior A). Every plane isometry is a homeomorphism, so e '' interior A = interior (e '' A). Moreover, e '' interior A ⊆ interior C iff e '' A ⊆ C: the forward implication follows by taking closures and using closedness of C; the reverse follows by taking interiors. Consequently the disjointness and containment conditions give exactly the usual packing convention. The feasible sizes, and therefore all five IsLeast questions, are unchanged. Scratch Lean proofs establish the packing equivalence for all four shape combinations used in the file.

sources_consulted: K. J. Nurmela and P. R. J. Östergård, More Optimal Packings of Equal Circles in a Square, Discrete & Computational Geometry 22 (1999), 439–457, especially the introduction, Table 2, and Section 3: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/PL00009472.pdf

review.notes: All five definitions/structure and all eleven theorems were checked. No substantive misformalization was found. Lean tests verified the Euclidean metric interpretation, the circle/open-ball identity, nonempty unit shapes, empty nonpositive square containers, exclusion of zero-sized containers for the stated positive packing counts, answer constraints, exact rational arithmetic, and the open/closed packing equivalences. Successful scratch files include /workspace/review/boundaries.lean and /workspace/review/verified_models.lean. The Pirl (1969) and Graham et al. (1998) primary full texts could not be accessed; the fifteen-circle formula, problem formulation, and recorded conjectural status were verified against the cited Wikipedia article and Friedman's visualization. The reviewed file was not modified.
